newsitem.title: albania: West scrambles to calm Albania as fighting rages.
newsitem.headline: West scrambles to calm Albania as fighting rages.

text.p: Troops battled armed insurgents in southern Albania on Wednesday as the West hastily prepared a diplomatic drive to calm the mass fury unleashed in Europe's poorest country by the disastrous collapse of speculative investment schemes.
While the army appeared to lose ground in a major clash, opposition politicians were calling on Europe and the U.S. to exert pressure on President Sali Berisha to help end the crisis.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said his country was watching the situation closely but so far had no plans to send troops to evacuate its citizens.

In the first major clash after three days of emergency rule, the Albanian army pulled back from fierce fighting near a village to the east of the Adriatic port of Sarande, eyewitnesses said. Four villagers and at least two soldiers were reported wounded in exchanges that lasted about 40 minutes.
"The people won. The army, about 60 soldiers, got in their trucks and drove away," Sarande's former prefect Dimitris Stefos told Reuters in Athens by telephone.

Rebels drove a tank captured from the army gleefully through the streets of Sarande. Hundreds of heavily armed men set up a defence line in the hills at the entrance to the town, saying they were determined to fight to the finish.

A fighter plane flew over the village of Livina near Sarande and smoke rose from the area just after it passed, witnesses said. Authorities denied allegations by two pilots who defected to Italy that they had been given orders to shoot at civilians. Opposition parties appealed to the West to force Berisha to negotiate.

The 11-party Forum for Democracy, grouped around the Socialists, successors to the communist party in what was for years Europe's most isolated and deeply Stalinist state, said it wanted an end to emergency rule and called for the West to link financial aid to political reform.
"Being convinced that the crisis has a political solution, we appeal to them to do their best to avoid a civil war in Albania," the group said in a statement.
Berisha on Tuesday rejected the opposition's call for government of "technocrats". He rejected any coalition grouping his ruling Democratic Party and the opposition Socialists.
The president issued no fresh political initiatives on Wednesday, but suggested an overnight curfew be shortened by three hours in Tirana and other areas unaffected by unrest.
Authorities announced that army chief of staff General Sheme Kosova had been dismissed and replaced by Major General Adem Copani, Berisha's personal military adviser.

A statement from the prime minister's office published in the newspaper Rilindja Demokratike said Kosova had been sacked for failing to ensure adequate security at military posts stormed and looted of their weapons by "terrorists".

The international community issued fresh expressions of concern about the crisis. Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok told reporters in Paris the European Union was sending his country's foreign minister to Albania on Friday for emergency talks.
A mission of the Council of Europe, the Strasbourg-based body overseeing human rights throughout the continent, was arriving in Tirana on Wednesday.
The delegation planned to meet Berisha and seek contact with all political forces during its two-day visit.
U.S. Defence Secretary Cohen, on a visit to Germany, told reporters no plans had been made to pull out the 1,000 or so American citizens in Albania.
"We are watching it,' he said, "but as of this time there are no military plans that have been instituted nor any need to call upon the U.S. military."
U.S. army General George Joulwan, commander of American and NATO forces in Europe, said the U.S. already had warships in the region and was in contact with the U.S. ambassador in Tirana.
Albanian troops have been pressing south from the capital Tirana since Monday to reinstate government authority in the region, which erupted in violence at the weekend.
Government officials said the army, backed by police, had secured roads to the flashpoint of Vlore on the Adriatic coast and the mountainous route between the inland town of Gjirokaster and Sarande.

In Vlore, two people were killed and 19 injured in gunfire, the Health Ministry said. Over 20 people are reported to have died in the town since fresh violence erupted there last Friday. Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said on Wednesday he had been told by his Albanian counterpart Tritan Shehu that the situation in Vlore, Sarande and the town of Delvine was "out of control". Rebels had captured three armoured vehicles, he added.
